title: Spherical Law of Cosines OQ-02: the Girard–Euler Excess Formula
description: Formal entry for OQ-02 of the parent gallery entry `spherical-law-of-cosines`: the Girard–Euler theorem, which identifies the area (in steradians) of a spherical triangle with its spherical excess $S = A + B + C - \pi$. A from-scratch measure-theoretic proof would require spherical-area/solid-angle infrastructure that Mathlib does not yet have (an estimated >1000 lines). Instead this file formalises, with 0 axioms and 0 sorries, the two arithmetic pillars on which every classical proof of Girard's theorem rests: (1) finite additivity of the excess under geodesic subdivision — a cevian split, the spherical quadrilateral ($n=4$) and pentagon ($n=5$) cases of the polygon excess formula; and (2) the lune-covering reduction deriving $S = A+B+C-\pi$ from the lune-area facts and the six-lune covering count. The genuinely geometric facts (lune areas $=2\theta$, supplementary angles at a subdivision point, the vertex-angle split, sphere area $4\pi$) enter as theorem hypotheses, so every result is an unconditional, machine-checked implication. 11 theorems, 1 definition, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.

meta.author: Girard, Euler, Todhunter
meta.assumptions: None counted as axioms: all 11 theorems are unconditional implications (0 sorries, 0 `axiom` declarations, 0 structure-encoded assumptions; `#print axioms` lists only propext/Classical.choice/Quot.sound). The substantive geometric content of Girard's theorem — that a lune of dihedral angle θ has area 2θ, that the six antipodal lunes cover the sphere with the triangle and its antipode triply covered, that the two angles at a geodesic subdivision point are supplementary, and that a vertex angle splits additively under a cevian — is supplied as theorem *hypotheses* rather than derived from a Mathlib spherical-area measure (which does not exist at v4.26.0). The file therefore proves the arithmetic backbone and lune reduction of Girard's theorem, not a self-contained measure-theoretic proof; this scoping is disclosed in the file header and the overview. The two pillars are independently meaningful: `sphericalExcess_additive_cevian` (and its quadrilateral/pentagon generalisations) is the finite-additivity property that forces excess to behave like an area, and `girard_euler_from_lunes` is the classical lune computation closing the formula.

sections.title: File Header and Setup
sections.summary: Documentation header stating OQ-02 (the Girard–Euler excess formula), explaining why a from-scratch measure-theoretic proof is out of Mathlib's current reach, and laying out the two pillars formalised here (finite additivity of the excess, and the lune-covering reduction). Imports only Mathlib.
sections.mathContext: Girard's theorem: $\operatorname{area}(\triangle) = A + B + C - \pi$ on the unit sphere, with area measured in steradians (solid angle). The excess $A+B+C-\pi$ is positive precisely because the sphere has positive Gaussian curvature $K=1$.

sections.title: The spherical excess
sections.summary: Defines `sphericalExcess A B C := A + B + C - π` (noncomputable, as it references `Real.pi`), records the definitional `@[simp]` lemma, and proves symmetry of the excess under relabelling of vertices.
sections.mathContext: The excess is the unique (up to scale) finitely additive, motion-invariant function of a spherical triangle's angles, which is why Girard's theorem identifies it with area.

sections.title: Pillar 1: finite additivity under subdivision
sections.summary: Proves `sphericalExcess_additive_cevian`: a cevian from a vertex to the opposite side splits a triangle into two whose excesses sum to the whole, given that the vertex angle splits (`C = C₁ + C₂`) and the two angles at the interior subdivision point are supplementary (`δ₁ + δ₂ = π`). Generalises to `sphericalExcess_quadrilateral` (the $n=4$ polygon case, area $=\sum\text{angles}-2\pi$, via a diagonal) and `sphericalExcess_pentagon` (the $n=5$ fan triangulation, area $=\sum\text{angles}-3\pi$).
sections.mathContext: Finite additivity is the structural reason the excess equals area: area is a finitely additive set function, the excess is a finitely additive function of geodesic polygons, and the two agree. The polygon formula $\operatorname{area} = (\sum\text{angles}) - (n-2)\pi$ follows by triangulation into $n-2$ triangles.

sections.title: Pillar 2: the lune-covering reduction (Girard's theorem)
sections.summary: Proves `girard_euler_from_lunes`: from the lune-area hypotheses (the antipodal lune pair at each vertex has area `4·angle`), the sphere area (`4π`), and the covering identity (the six lunes total `sphereArea + 4S`, since they cover the triangle and its antipode triply and everything else once), Girard's formula `S = A + B + C - π` follows by linear arithmetic.
sections.mathContext: Classical lune proof (Todhunter §99–101): a lune of dihedral angle θ has area 2θ; the three great circles through the triangle's sides create three antipodal lune pairs whose six lunes tile the sphere, overcounting the triangle T and its antipode T′ (each area S) by a factor of three. Hence $4A+4B+4C = 4\pi + 4S$.

sections.title: Consequences of Girard's formula
sections.summary: Five corollaries of Girard's formula: positive area ⟺ angle sum > π (`pos_area_iff_angle_sum_gt_pi`); the flat/Euclidean limit (zero excess ⟺ angle sum = π, `excess_eq_zero_iff`); the non-negativity criterion (`excess_nonneg_iff`); the hemisphere bound (each angle < π ⟹ excess < 2π, `excess_lt_two_pi`); and strict monotonicity of the area in a single angle (`excess_strictMono_left`).
sections.mathContext: These extract the qualitative geometry encoded in Girard's formula: spherical triangles are 'fat' (angle sum exceeds π), degenerate to Euclidean as the excess vanishes, are bounded in area by a hemisphere (2π steradians), and grow in area monotonically with any opening angle.

overview.historicalContext: Albert Girard stated the spherical-excess area formula in 1629 (Invention nouvelle en l'algèbre), and it was independently rediscovered and rigorously treated by Euler (De mensura angulorum solidorum, 1781) and later Lambert and Legendre. It is the spherical counterpart of the Gauss–Bonnet theorem: on a surface of constant curvature K, the area of a geodesic triangle equals (angle excess)/K, and on the unit sphere K=1 gives area = A+B+C−π directly. The formula is the historical seed of the Gauss–Bonnet theorem and of the modern notion that curvature is measured by angle defect.
overview.problemStatement: **OQ-02**: Prove the spherical excess formula — the sum of the angles of a spherical triangle exceeds π by the solid angle (area) of the triangle, i.e. $A + B + C - \pi = \operatorname{area}(\triangle)$ in steradians. This is the Girard–Euler theorem, connecting spherical geometry to solid-angle computation.
overview.text: Prove the spherical excess formula: the sum of angles of a spherical triangle exceeds π by the solid angle (area) of the triangle. That is, A + B + C − π = area(△), where area is measured in steradians. This is the Girard-Euler theorem, connecting spherical geometry to solid angle computation.
overview.proofStrategy: The classical proof has two separable components. (1) **Finite additivity**: subdividing a spherical triangle by a geodesic cevian splits it into two triangles whose angle data satisfy `C = C₁ + C₂` (vertex split) and `δ₁ + δ₂ = π` (supplementary angles at the interior point); the excesses then add. This file proves the additivity identity and its quadrilateral and pentagon generalisations by `linarith`/`ring` once the two angle relations are taken as hypotheses. (2) **Normalisation via lunes**: a lune of dihedral angle θ has area 2θ, and the six antipodal lunes generated by the triangle's three side great circles tile the sphere while triple-covering the triangle and its antipode; equating the two expressions for the total lune area gives `S = A+B+C−π`. This file proves the reduction `girard_euler_from_lunes` from the lune-area and covering-count hypotheses. The genuinely measure-theoretic facts (lune area = 2θ, the covering multiplicity, sphere area = 4π) are isolated as hypotheses because Mathlib lacks a spherical-area measure; building one is estimated at >1000 lines and is the documented blocker to a fully self-contained proof.
keyInsights: Girard's theorem factors cleanly into a purely arithmetic 'additivity' part and a 'lune normalisation' part; this file proves both, isolating the missing measure theory into named hypotheses.

Finite additivity under a cevian uses exactly two geometric facts: the vertex angle splits (C = C₁ + C₂) and the two angles at the subdivision point are supplementary (δ₁ + δ₂ = π). The resulting cancellation '+π − 2π = −π' is the entire content.
The same additivity argument yields the spherical polygon formula area = (Σ angles) − (n−2)π; the n=4 (quadrilateral, via a diagonal) and n=5 (pentagon, via a fan) cases are proved explicitly.
The lune reduction is one linear equation: 4A + 4B + 4C = 4π + 4S, because the six antipodal lunes (areas 4A, 4B, 4C) cover the sphere (4π) plus the triangle and its antipode twice extra each (4S).

Girard's formula immediately yields the qualitative geometry of the sphere: angle sum > π ⟺ positive area, zero excess ⟺ Euclidean (flat) limit, area < 2π (hemisphere bound), and area strictly increasing in each opening angle.

Mathlib at v4.26.0 has no spherical-area / solid-angle measure, so a from-scratch proof of the lune-area facts is the >1000-line blocker; the hypothesis-based reduction is the honest, verified intermediate.
prerequisites: Spherical geometry (geodesic triangles, dihedral angles, lunes, antipodal map)
The notion of solid angle / area in steradians on the unit sphere
Elementary real arithmetic (the proofs themselves are `linarith` / `ring`)

conclusion.summary: Formalises the arithmetic backbone and lune reduction of the Girard–Euler spherical-excess theorem with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. Pillar 1 (`sphericalExcess_additive_cevian`, plus the quadrilateral and pentagon polygon cases) proves the finite additivity that forces the excess to behave like an area. Pillar 2 (`girard_euler_from_lunes`) proves the classical lune computation `S = A+B+C−π` from the lune-area and covering-count hypotheses. Five corollaries extract the qualitative geometry (angle-sum/area dichotomy, flat limit, non-negativity, hemisphere bound, monotonicity). The measure-theoretic identification of area with solid angle is isolated into theorem hypotheses, because Mathlib has no spherical-area measure at v4.26.0; this scoping is disclosed throughout.
conclusion.implications: Girard's theorem is the constant-curvature K=1 case of the Gauss–Bonnet theorem and the prototype for measuring curvature by angle defect. The finite-additivity pillar proved here is exactly the structural fact that makes 'area = excess' inevitable once a single normalisation is fixed, and it generalises verbatim to the spherical polygon formula area = (Σ angles) − (n−2)π (n=4 and n=5 proved). The lune-reduction pillar reduces the remaining content to four clearly-stated geometric inputs, turning the open formalisation gap into a precise statement: supply a Mathlib spherical-area measure together with the lune-area lemma `area(lune θ) = 2θ` and the six-lune covering count, and `girard_euler_from_lunes` closes the full theorem with no further work. This makes the entry both a usable verified result and an exact specification of the missing infrastructure.
openQuestions: Build a Mathlib spherical-area (solid-angle) measure on S² and prove the lune-area lemma area(lune θ) = 2θ and the six-lune covering count, discharging the hypotheses of `girard_euler_from_lunes` to obtain a fully self-contained Girard theorem (the documented >1000-line blocker).

Prove the general spherical n-gon excess formula area = (Σ interior angles) − (n−2)π by induction on a fan triangulation, generalising the explicit quadrilateral (n=4) and pentagon (n=5) cases proved here.

Derive the dual angular Girard form and connect to the parent `spherical-law-of-cosines` `SphericalTriangle`/`angleC` API, so that the additive cevian relations (C = C₁ + C₂, δ₁ + δ₂ = π) are themselves proved from the projection-inner-product definition of the dihedral angle rather than assumed.

Formalise the hyperbolic counterpart (constant curvature K = −1): a hyperbolic triangle has area = π − (A + B + C) (the angle defect), and state both as instances of a single constant-curvature Gauss–Bonnet area law area = (A + B + C − π)/K.

Quantify L'Huilier's theorem as a side-based formula for the excess, $\tan(S/4) = \sqrt{\tan(s/2)\tan((s-a)/2)\tan((s-b)/2)\tan((s-c)/2)}$, giving the area directly from the spherical side lengths a, b, c (semiperimeter s) — the spherical analogue of Heron's formula.
